# MT7628KN Wi-Fi Extender

> 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi extender (MediaTek MT7628KN, eCos firmware) with an HTTP configuration page, a small HTTP API and a Telnet console.

Use this device's current HTTP origin; no fixed IP is required. Credentials, when set, come from the owner. This file contains no credentials and is readable without signing in.

Ask the owner before changing connectivity, credentials, restarting or writing firmware. Never infer authorization from this file.

## Factory defaults

- Device network: open (no password), named "Extender-" followed by the Wi-Fi MAC in uppercase without colons, for example Extender-A03E9C1D0E54.
- Mode: Ethernet router (MODE=gateway). The device network is 192.168.11.1/24 and hands out 192.168.11.100-199 by DHCP, so a phone or laptop that joins it gets an address and reaches http://192.168.11.1/ with no cable and no manual address. The Ethernet port is the Internet uplink: it takes an address from the router on the other end by DHCP (wan_address in the state) and the device network is behind NAT. The page is also reachable at that Ethernet address from the upstream network.
- Admin: user "admin", no password; the page opens without signing in. Telnet is disabled.
- WireGuard: disabled, with a new device key; the server must be given the new public key.
- Rescue address: in the bridged modes (ap, repeater) 192.168.11.1 is always present on the device side next to its DHCP address; in the router modes the device network itself is the way in.
- Holding the reset button for more than 4 seconds restores these defaults and restarts (about one minute). A short press only restarts.

## Find the device

1. Factory defaults: join the open "Extender-..." network; your client gets a 192.168.11.x address by DHCP; open http://192.168.11.1/. This works with or without the Ethernet cable.
2. Configured device: join its device network. In router modes (gateway, router) use the gateway address your client received (the device's LAN address, for example 10.0.1.1 or 192.168.11.1). In bridged modes (ap, repeater) the device has a DHCP address from the upstream router: find the lease for its MAC there, or set a static address in 192.168.11.0/24 on your client (wired or Wi-Fi) and use http://192.168.11.1/.
3. From the upstream network (the far end of the Ethernet cable), in gateway mode the device answers at the address it leased there (look for its MAC in the upstream router's DHCP leases).
4. By name: the device answers mDNS as http://extender.local/ (or http://<mdns_name>.local/ when renamed) from clients on its networks and on the network it gets its address from. Not every client resolves .local (Android before 12 often does not); fall back to the steps above.
5. Confirm with GET /wifi_state.html: JSON with "chip":"MT7628KN".

## Set up from factory defaults

Do these in order. After each POST, check the response is OK.

1. Inspect: GET /wifi_state.html. Note uplink_type, ethernet, networks[], admin_password_set.
2. Secure administration first: POST /admin_apply.html USER=admin&PASSWORD=<new>&CONFIRM=<new>&CURRENT= . Then use HTTP Basic authentication with these credentials on every later request (except /llms.txt).
3. Choose where the Internet comes from and what each Wi-Fi network is, and apply everything with one POST /setup_apply.html (see "Internet and networks" in the API reference). The device restarts (about one minute).
   - Internet: UPLINK=cable (the Ethernet cable goes to the router or modem) or UPLINK=wifi (GET /wifi_scan.html, pick the network; use its channel as CHANNEL and its security: WPA2PSK/AES = wpa2, WPA1PSKWPA2PSK/... = mixed, NONE = open; WPA3/SAE and enterprise are unsupported).
   - Each network n (1..COUNT, up to 7; network 1 always exists) is TYPEn=nat (its own range ADDRESSn with DHCP, behind this device) or TYPEn=bridge (clients join the Internet side's network and get addresses from its router).
   Examples (password 12345678 is only an example):
   - Cable, one NAT network (the factory layout): UPLINK=cable&CHANNEL=6&COUNT=1&SSID1=Home&SECURITY1=wpa2&PASSWORD1=12345678&TYPE1=nat&ADDRESS1=192.168.11.1/24&REACH1=device
   - Cable, extend the existing network (access point): UPLINK=cable&CHANNEL=6&COUNT=1&SSID1=Home&SECURITY1=wpa2&PASSWORD1=12345678&TYPE1=bridge
   - Wi-Fi uplink, own NAT network: UPLINK=wifi&UPLINK_SSID=<network>&UPLINK_SECURITY=wpa2&UPLINK_PASSWORD=<password>&CHANNEL=<uplink channel>&ETHERNET=net1&COUNT=1&SSID1=Home&SECURITY1=wpa2&PASSWORD1=12345678&TYPE1=nat&ADDRESS1=10.0.1.1/24&REACH1=device
   - Wi-Fi uplink, repeat the network (repeater): as above with TYPE1=bridge&ETHERNET=internet . With a Wi-Fi uplink and a bridged network, unplug any Ethernet cable to the same network first (it would make a loop).
   - Mixed: networks may be NAT and bridge at the same time, for example a bridged network for the house and a NAT guest network: ...&COUNT=2&TYPE1=bridge&SSID2=Guest&SECURITY2=wpa2&PASSWORD2=12345678&TYPE2=nat&ADDRESS2=10.0.2.1/24&ISOLATE2=1
4. Reconnect. A NAT network hands out addresses by DHCP and the device is at its ADDRESSn host (for example http://192.168.11.1/). In a bridged network the device has an address from the upstream router (find its MAC in the router's leases) and also answers at http://192.168.11.1/ from a client set to a static 192.168.11.x address.
5. Verify: GET /wifi_state.html shows uplink_type, ethernet, networks[] with the types and addresses you set, admin_password_set=1 and, when network 1 uses WPA2, telnet=1. With a Wi-Fi uplink, uplink_status must be "connected"; "disconnected" usually means a wrong uplink password or channel. Finally test traffic (for example a web request) from a client on each network.

DHCP and cables: a NAT network 1 with DHCP1=1 also hands out addresses on the Ethernet port when ETHERNET=net1. If that port is cabled to an existing network (for example the home LAN), use DHCP1=0 or ETHERNET=internet: otherwise the device becomes a second DHCP server there. Ask the owner if unsure.

Telnet (TCP 23, same admin credentials) becomes available only with an admin password and network 1 on WPA2. It is for diagnostics and firmware installation; see Firmware tests and recovery below.

If any network will use VIAn=wg, set up WireGuard first (section below) and confirm it is connected.

## Optional: WireGuard

The device can join a WireGuard server as a peer (initiator only, one server). Off by default; needs an admin password. The page and Telnet are then reachable at the tunnel address.

1. GET /wifi_state.html and read wireguard.public_key (generated on the device, new after every factory reset; the private key never leaves it).
2. On the server, add that key as a peer with AllowedIPs = <tunnel address>/32. After a factory reset the device has a new key: replace the PublicKey of its existing peer on the server (the old key must stop working) instead of adding a second peer.
3. POST /wg_apply.html ENABLED=1&ADDRESS=<tunnel address/prefix, e.g. 10.8.0.30/24>&PEER_PUBLIC_KEY=<server public key>&ENDPOINT=<server host>&PORT=<51820>&KEEPALIVE=25 . The device saves and restarts.
4. After about one minute, GET /wifi_state.html: wireguard.state "connected" and a small wireguard.handshake_age mean the tunnel is up. The device needs Internet access for SNTP (pool.ntp.org) before its first handshake.

## Optional: startup script

Up to 16 console commands, one per line, run once at every boot, about 20 seconds after start, in order, exactly as typed at the Telnet prompt (submenu names first, for example "net route add 10.9.0.0 255.255.0.0 192.168.1.2"). POST /startup_apply.html SCRIPT=<the whole script, lines separated by newlines> (URL-encode the newlines as %0A; the script replaces the previous one). GET /wifi_state.html shows each line and its result at the last boot in startup[]. reboot is not available to the script.

## Recovery

- Lost credentials or a broken configuration: hold the reset button for more than 4 seconds, then start again from factory defaults.
- Device unreachable after a Wi-Fi change: reconnect to the configured device network; if it is gone, connect by Ethernet and use the DHCP address or http://192.168.11.1/.
- A power cycle always boots the installed firmware.

## API reference

MT7628KN Wi-Fi extender. All paths are relative to the current device origin. When an admin password is set, every page except /llms.txt requires HTTP Basic authentication with the admin user and password (sent unencrypted over HTTP). With no admin password, no authentication is required. No cloud service is used.

Requests that change settings use POST with application/x-www-form-urlencoded fields. Responses are OK when accepted, or ERROR: followed by an explanation. GET requests to these endpoints do not change settings.

### Read current state

GET /wifi_state.html returns JSON:
- busy (0 or 1), revision (apply counter), error (0 on success; -3 means saving failed), stage, saved (1 when the last apply was written and verified in flash).
- layout (nat: every active network is NAT; bridge: all bridged; mixed), uplink_type (cable or wifi), ethernet (wan: the cable is the Internet; net1: the port is part of network 1; internet: the port is bridged with the Internet side).
- mode (gateway, ap, repeater or router: the underlying mode of the older endpoints), ssid (device network), device_security (open or wpa2), channel.
- uplink (uplink SSID in repeater and router modes), security (uplink driver authentication name), uplink_status (repeater only: driver connection text, for example "Connected" or "Disconnected").
- admin_user, admin_password_set (0 or 1), telnet (1 when Telnet logins are accepted).
- chip, version, build (UNIX time), uptime (seconds), mdns_name (the .local name; empty: mDNS off), open_fds (open descriptors, out of 256), wss_error (the last WSS problem, empty if none).
- firmware: busy, state and error of the last firmware check, test or installation.
- lan (router and gateway modes): address (IPv4/prefix), dhcp (0 or 1). wan_address (gateway mode): the address the Ethernet uplink got by DHCP, empty until it has one.
- networks: seven objects (id 1-7) with enabled, ssid, security (open or wpa2), isolate (0 or 1), type (nat or bridge), address (the NAT range, empty for bridge), reach, internet and via (wan or wg); ids 2-7 also schedule (HH:MM-HH:MM or empty) and off_by_schedule (1 while outside the window).
- time (local HH:MM, empty while unknown) and tz_offset (minutes from UTC).
- wireguard: enabled, address (tunnel address/prefix), peer_public_key, endpoint, port, watchdog (minutes, 0: off), keepalive, dns, transport (udp or wss), wss_path, wss_name, wss_key, preshared_key_set, public_key (this device, base64; new after every factory reset), state (off, starting, clock, handshake, connected or error), status, handshake_age (seconds, -1 before the first), rx_bytes and tx_bytes.

Passwords are never returned.

### Scan for networks

GET /wifi_scan.html runs a site survey (about 3 seconds) and returns JSON {"error": "", "raw": "<driver table>"}. error is "busy" while settings are being applied. raw is a fixed-width table whose header line starts with "Ch  SSID  BSSID  Security  Siganl(%)W-Mode"; locate columns by the header positions. SSIDs with non-ASCII bytes appear as 0x followed by hex (decode as UTF-8). Empty SSIDs are hidden networks. Security values such as WPA2PSK/AES map to wpa2, WPA1PSKWPA2PSK/TKIPAES to mixed and NONE to open; WPA3/SAE and enterprise networks are unsupported.

### Internet and networks

POST /setup_apply.html sets everything in one request; the device saves and restarts. Fields:
- UPLINK: cable or wifi. CHANNEL: 1-13 (with a Wi-Fi uplink, the uplink's channel; all networks share it).
- Wi-Fi uplink: UPLINK_SSID (1-32 bytes), UPLINK_SECURITY (wpa2, mixed or open), UPLINK_PASSWORD (8-63 ASCII; empty keeps the stored one for the same SSID), UPLINK_BSSID (optional aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff), ETHERNET (net1: the port is part of network 1, needs network 1 as NAT and no bridged network; internet: the port is bridged with the Internet side).
- COUNT: 1-7 networks (the radio has 8 beacons and a Wi-Fi uplink uses one).
- For each n from 1 to COUNT: SSIDn (1-32 bytes); SECURITYn (open or wpa2); PASSWORDn (8-63 ASCII; empty keeps the stored key when the network already used WPA2); TYPEn (nat or bridge); ISOLATEn (1: clients cannot see each other).
- For NAT networks: ADDRESSn (IPv4/prefix 8-30, the device's address; DHCP hands out .100-.199); INTERNETn (1 default, or 0); REACHn (comma list of what the network may open connections to: device, net1 ... net7, lan (the local network on the Internet side), wg; empty: only the Internet); VIAn (wan default, or wg: Internet through the WireGuard tunnel, dropped if the tunnel is down; DNS offered is the WireGuard DNS, default 1.1.1.1).
- DHCP1: 1 (default) or 0, for network 1 when it is NAT and no network is bridged.
- SCHEDn (networks 2-7, optional): HH:MM-HH:MM in local time (see ACTION=time); the network is on only inside that window, which may cross midnight (22:00-06:00); empty: always on. Network 1 always stays on. Until the device knows the time (SNTP over the Internet) no network is turned off.
Ranges overlapping each other or the WireGuard network are refused. Others can always open connections into a NAT network and get replies; use REACH on the other side to allow the reverse. Invalid fields are rejected before anything changes.

The endpoints below (/wifi_apply.html, /networks_apply.html) are older shortcuts for the same settings and keep working.

### Apply Wi-Fi settings

POST /wifi_apply.html with:
- MODE: gateway, ap, repeater or router. gateway (factory default): Ethernet is the WAN (DHCP client) with NAT; the device network (Wi-Fi) uses LAN_ADDRESS (default 192.168.11.1/24) and, with LAN_DHCP=1, hands out .100-.199. ap and repeater bridge clients to the upstream network (ap: Ethernet uplink; repeater: Wi-Fi uplink), use upstream DHCP for the management address and run no DHCP server. router (WISP): Wi-Fi uplink as WAN with NAT; the device's own network uses LAN_ADDRESS and, with LAN_DHCP=1, hands out .100-.199. Changing to or from router or gateway saves and restarts the device instead of applying live.
- LAN_ADDRESS: router and gateway, IPv4/prefix 8-30 (default 10.0.1.1/24 for router, 192.168.11.1/24 for gateway). LAN_DHCP: router and gateway, 1 (default) or 0; use 0 when the Ethernet port is cabled to a network that already has a DHCP server.
- UPLINK_BSSID: optional for repeater and router, aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff, pins the uplink to one access point; empty lets the driver choose by name.
- SSID: device network name, 1-32 UTF-8 bytes, no control characters.
- DEVICE_SECURITY: open or wpa2.
- PASSWORD: device WPA2-Personal password, 8-63 printable ASCII characters. With DEVICE_SECURITY=wpa2, an empty PASSWORD keeps the current password (only if the network already uses WPA2). Ignored for open.
- CHANNEL: 1-13. In repeater mode use the channel of the uplink network.
- UPLINK_SSID: repeater and router, 1-32 UTF-8 bytes.
- UPLINK_SECURITY: repeater and router: wpa2 (AES), mixed (WPA/WPA2 TKIP/AES) or open.
- UPLINK_PASSWORD: 8-63 printable ASCII characters for secured uplinks. Empty keeps the stored password when UPLINK_SSID is unchanged.

Settings are saved to flash and applied without a restart. Invalid fields are rejected before anything changes. OK means accepted, not connected: poll /wifi_state.html until busy is 0 and revision has increased, then require error=0 and saved=1 and verify mode, ssid, channel, uplink and, in repeater mode, uplink_status. A wrong uplink password keeps the device network running and shows a disconnected uplink_status. Also test traffic from a Wi-Fi client.

Access point mode needs Ethernet to the router. Repeater mode uses wireless backhaul: disconnect an Ethernet uplink to the same network before applying to avoid a bridge loop. Reconnect to the configured device SSID if Wi-Fi drops; the DHCP address may change.

### Wi-Fi networks

POST /networks_apply.html. COUNT: number of active SSIDs, 1-7 (the radio has 8 beacons and a Wi-Fi uplink uses one; network 1 is the device network from wifi_apply). ISOLATE1: 1 isolates clients of network 1 from each other. For each n from 2 to COUNT: SSIDn (1-32 bytes); SECURITYn open or wpa2; PASSWORDn (8-63 ASCII; empty keeps the stored key when the network already used WPA2); ADDRESSn (router mode only: IPv4/prefix 8-30 makes it a routed network with its own DHCP pool .100-.199 and NAT; empty bridges it with network 1); INTERNETn 1 (default) or 0; REACHn comma list of device, lan, net2 ... net7, wg (what the network may open connections to; empty: only the Internet); ISOLATEn 1 or 0; VIAn wan (default) or wg: Internet traffic leaves through the WireGuard tunnel, translated to this device's tunnel address; if the tunnel is down that traffic is dropped, never sent to the WAN (WireGuard must be enabled and configured before this request and the server must forward and masquerade; DNS offered is the WireGuard DNS, default 1.1.1.1). Ranges overlapping the LAN, another routed network or the WireGuard network are refused. Others can always open connections into a routed network and get replies; use REACH on the other side to allow the reverse. Saves and restarts the device. All networks share the radio and channel; with a Wi-Fi uplink the channel follows the uplink.

### Administration

POST /admin_apply.html with USER (1-31 printable ASCII characters, no spaces or colons), PASSWORD and CONFIRM (equal; 8-63 printable ASCII characters without spaces, or both empty to remove the password) and CURRENT (the current admin password; required when one is set). Credentials are saved to flash immediately and apply to HTTP and Telnet. After setting a password, sign in again with the new credentials. Removing the password disables Telnet.

### System

POST /system_apply.html with ACTION=reboot (restart), ACTION=factory (erase settings, restore factory defaults and restart), ACTION=time&TZ=<minutes from UTC, -720 to 840, default -180> (local time for network schedules) or ACTION=name&NAME=<name> (the mDNS host name: 1-63 letters, digits or "-", not at the ends; empty turns mDNS off; saved without restarting; factory default "extender"). The connection drops; the device returns after about one minute. Factory defaults: Ethernet router mode with the open network "Extender-<Wi-Fi MAC>" at 192.168.11.1/24 (DHCP), no admin password, Telnet disabled, WireGuard disabled with a new device key. The reset button does the same when held for more than 4 seconds; a short press restarts.

### WireGuard

POST /wg_apply.html with ENABLED (0 or 1), ADDRESS (this device's IPv4 address and prefix in the tunnel, prefix 8-32; the prefix is routed through wg0), PEER_PUBLIC_KEY (the server's WireGuard public key, 44 base64 characters), ENDPOINT (server host name or IPv4 address), PORT (1-65535, usually 51820), KEEPALIVE (0-3600 seconds; 25 recommended behind NAT) PRESHARED_KEY (44 base64 characters, empty for none, or "keep" to keep the stored one) and DNS (optional IPv4 address, default 1.1.1.1: the DNS server that DHCP offers to networks whose Internet goes through the tunnel, since the upstream router's DNS is not reachable from there; absent keeps the stored one). Optional: WATCHDOG (0, the default, turns it off; 5-1440 minutes: without a WireGuard session for that long, counted from start-up or the last connected moment, the device restarts and retries from scratch; absent keeps the stored value). TRANSPORT (udp, or wss to carry WireGuard over wstunnel: a WebSocket over TLS 1.3 to ENDPOINT port 443, delivered by the server to 127.0.0.1:PORT; for networks that block UDP. If WSS does not connect within 3 minutes the device falls back to UDP until the next restart, so it stays reachable), WSS_PATH (WebSocket path, for example /wstunnel/events), WSS_NAME (TLS server name and Host header; empty: ENDPOINT) and WSS_KEY (the server certificate's Ed25519 public key, 64 hex characters: the only thing trusted, no certificate authority). Absent optional fields keep their stored value. Enabling requires ADDRESS, PEER_PUBLIC_KEY, ENDPOINT and an admin password. Settings are saved and the device restarts. The client is initiator only: it rekeys every 2 minutes and does not answer handshakes started by the server, so use a keepalive. Before the first handshake it gets the time by SNTP from pool.ntp.org (WireGuard rejects stale timestamps). The device key is generated by the firmware; it is never exported or replaced through the API.

### Log

GET /log.html returns the last console messages as text (an 8 KB ring, oldest first): WireGuard, WSS, mDNS, DHCP and network events. POST /system_apply.html ACTION=log&SERVER=<a.b.c.d[:port]> also sends every console line as syslog over UDP (facility user, severity info, tagged with the mDNS name) to that server, default port 514; empty SERVER turns it off. Saved without restarting. State: log_server.

### Settings file (backup and restore)

GET /config_backup.html returns every setting as text, one NAME=value per line, starting with "#PROFILE". It contains the Wi-Fi, uplink and admin passwords: keep it private. The WireGuard device key and the entropy seed are never included and never replaced, so a restored device keeps its own key (its server peer stays valid).
POST /config_restore.html as multipart/form-data with the file in the field "config" (up to 16000 bytes, a file from config_backup) applies every setting in it, saves and restarts. Needs an admin password; the restored file may set a different one (use the restored credentials afterwards). Ask the owner before restoring: it replaces the current settings.

### Startup script

POST /startup_apply.html with SCRIPT: the whole script, one command per line (\n or \r\n; up to 16 lines of printable ASCII, up to 200 characters each; empty lines are kept as empty lines, lines not given are cleared). The older form COMMAND1 to COMMAND16 sets single lines (empty clears a line; absent keeps it). Saved without restarting; they run at every boot, about 20 seconds after start, in order, as if typed at CMD> (submenu names first, e.g. "net route add <net> <mask> <gateway>" or "cfg set <NAME> <value>"). State: startup is a list of 16 objects (one per line) with command and result ("pending", "ok", "unknown command", "incomplete", "error N", or empty for an empty line). A failing line does not stop the following ones. reboot is not part of the command tree, so it cannot run at startup. Commands that change the saved configuration (cfg set, cfg prof ...) run at every boot; prefer the API for permanent settings.

### Firmware update over HTTP

POST /firmware_apply.html?ACTION=check|test|install as multipart/form-data with the image in the field "firmware" (a zxrouter uImage for this device, as built by the firmware's CI). Needs an admin password (HTTP Basic). check validates header, checksums and target and writes nothing. test runs the image in RAM; a restart or power cycle returns to the installed firmware. install writes only the firmware partition (boot loader, settings and Wi-Fi calibration are kept), verifies it and restarts. The response is OK when the image was accepted; follow progress in GET /wifi_state.html firmware.state (queued, checking, checked, erasing, programming, verifying, installed, booting or failed, with firmware.error). Prefer test before install; never cut power while installing.

### Firmware tests and recovery

Telnet uses TCP 23 and accepts logins only when an admin password is set and the device network uses WPA2; otherwise it explains why and refuses. Authenticate with the admin credentials supplied by the owner. The serial console needs no login. At CMD>, use help and ramboot status. Use up to leave submenus.

ramboot check <TFTP-server> <file.img> downloads and validates a complete uImage including its header. ramboot boot <TFTP-server> <file.img> downloads, validates and executes it in RAM, dropping connections. Neither command installs firmware. Use a compatible image and an authorized TFTP server.

Normal flash driver writes are blocked except for the explicit configuration-save operation, limited to config data at offsets 0x31000–0x35fff. Erasing preserves other bytes of its physical sector 0x30000–0x3ffff. Bootloader/environment and calibration are outside this sector. A power cycle boots the installed firmware; hardware watchdog recovery requires compatible test firmware that preserves the watchdog. A network-only hang may need a power cycle. Never use direct flash-write commands during an inspection.

### Explicit firmware installation

ramboot install-check <TFTP-server> <file.img> validates the complete uImage and flash geometry without writing. ramboot flash-info reports CRC32 checks of boot/environment, config sector and calibration. ramboot flash-read <offset> <length> reads up to 256 bytes of the config sector for a private backup.

Only with explicit owner authorization, ramboot install <TFTP-server> <file.img> CONFIRM-FLASH downloads and validates the image, erases firmware blocks starting at 0x50000, programs and verifies the payload, then commits the uImage header last and verifies the complete result. Check ramboot status for state=installed, busy=0, error=none. It does not reboot or save configuration. Never interrupt power during installation. Power cycling after successful installation starts the new resident image.
